title: Not all black holes are born in supernova explosions. Some stars simply implode
excerpt: The findings were published by a team of researchers from the California Institute of Technology.
content:
Stay updated with ThePrint:

New Delhi: Astronomers have found evidence that a large number of black holes could have formed when massive stars collapsed into themselves without exploding into supernovae.

The team of researchers from the California Institute of Technology, or Caltech, published their findings in the journal Physical Review D on 10 November. Their conclusion is based on the analysis of data about gravitational waves collected by the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observator (LIGO) and two other detectors, Virgo and KAGRA (Kamioka Gravitational Wave Detector).

For years, scientists have claimed that black holes were the result of massive supernova explosions. When stars no longer had capacity to fuel their inner nuclear fusion, their cores would collapse, and their out layers would expand, triggering the explosion. However, new data suggests that some large stars that fail to turn into supernovae, can also turn into black holes.

“A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun. Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin—they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract,” Katerina Chatziioannou, a professor of physics at Caltech, said in a university statement.

Failed supernovae

So far, scientists have not found any evidence of failed supernovae, they only have theories. However, according to some astrophysicists, there is a large population of such stars that “imploded” instead of exploding. Many of these might be about 10 times the mass of the sun and they might have merged into black holes in pairs.

“We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time,” lead author Isaac Legred from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign said. “But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.”

Scientists are still trying to make sense of such mysteries using gravitational waves, ripples in space that are produced by the movements of large celestial objects, such as two black holes that might be orbiting each other only to eventually collide.

“We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it’s challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky. With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting,” Legred said in a statement.
